# Thermoelectric Properties of Materials
### **Thermoelectric Figure of Merit**
In addition a low electrical resistivity \(\rho\) (or high electrical conductivity \(\sigma\)) and low thermal conductivity \(\kappa\) is required for high efficiency.

### **Thermoelectric Quality Factor**
Nearly all good thermoelectric materials are heavily doped semiconductors: semiconductors which have so many free electrons that they have many properties similar to metals. Because all the properties in \(zT\), Seebeck coefficient, electrical resistivity and thermal conductivity depend on charge carrier concentration in a conflicting manner (see figure) achieving high \(zT\) in a material typically requires optimizing the charge carrier concentration.

This shows the quality of a thermoelectric material can be divided into the electronic contribution to the quality factor, \(B_\mathrm{E}\), which is determined by the [weighted mobility](https://thermoelectrics.matsci.northwestern.edu/thermoelectrics/index.html#mu_w) \(\mu_\mathrm{w}\), and its thermal contribution to the quality factor, which is the [lattice thermal conductivity](https://thermoelectrics.matsci.northwestern.edu/thermoelectrics/index.html#kappa_L) \(\kappa_\mathrm{L}\).[ 6, 42] These materials properties can be easily evaluated (or at least estimated) from measurements of Seebeck coefficient, electrical conductivity and thermal conductivity, [14], and therefore the potential of a new material can be estimated from a single sample where charge transport is dominated by a single type of charge carrier (electrons or holes).

In most good thermoelectric materials phonon scattering of electrons dominates leading to a \(T^{3/2}\) dependence of \(\mu_\mathrm{w}\) which makes \(B_\mathrm{E}\) largely temperature independent.

# Electronic Properties of Materials
### Grain Boundary Resistance
![zT vs n](https://thermoelectrics.matsci.northwestern.edu/graphics/thermoelectrics/ChargedInterface.jpg)

**Grain boundary electrical resistance in thermoelectric matreials is likely caused by electrically charged interfaces that trap and/or repel charge carriers [10].**

[Thermal boundary or Kapitza Resistance](https://thermoelectrics.matsci.northwestern.edu/thermoelectrics/index.html#Kapitza) is treated similarly and discussed in the section on [thermal properties of materials](https://thermoelectrics.matsci.northwestern.edu/thermoelectrics/index.html#Kapitza).

Regardless of the exact physical model, the phenomenological bricklayer model works well to characterize the electrical [10] and thermal [39] conductivity in polycrystalline thermoelectric materials. Because many good thermoelectric materials, such as PbTe and Bi₂Te₃ are heavily doped and have high dielectric constant grain boundary effects can be small and overlooked; it enables dense, polycrystalline pellets of material to be analyzed like they were single crystals. However many thermoelectrics with lighter elements, such as Mg₃Sb₂, have significant grain boundary contributions to the resistivity, even at high temperature such that reducing the grain size dramatically improves the \(zT\) [10].

# Thermal Properties of Thermoelectric Materials
### Thermal Boundary - Kapitza Resistance
A microscopic treatment of [low angle grain boundaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grain_boundary#High_and_low_angle_boundaries), made of arrays of dislocations (low energy structure), gives the AMM result in the long wavelength limit and a frequency dependence for phonons with wavelength small enough to interact with the dislocations [24].

The ideal thermoelectric material is then one which is a "Electron Crystal - Phonon Glass" [1] where high mobility electrons are free to transport charge and heat but the phonons are disrupted at the atomic scale from transporting heat.

In this review, we focus on the physical and chemical properties of various thermoelectric materials. ## [Characterizations of thermoelectric ceramics](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780323907613000024) ### Abstract Thermoelectric devices made of thermoelectric materials also have a series of characteristics such as small size, lightweight, no noise, no vibration, no mechanical parts, accuracy and reliability, and no environmental pollution. ## [Beyond 3D-traditional materials thermoelectric materials](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780128199848000072) ### Abstract Thermoelectric materials are characterized by figure of merit ( _zT_) and they show large Seebeck coefficient, high electrical conductivity, and low thermal conductivity. These thermoelectric properties can be easily tailored by tacking dopants, introducing defects, forming nanostructures, and creating quantum dots. ## [Recent progress on graphene-analogous 2D nanomaterials: Properties, modeling and applications](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0079642518300938) ### 4.5Thermoelectric Among all the GE-analogous 2D nanomaterials, there are several materials that possess a unique feature, i.e., they have excellent electronic properties but low thermal conductivity, thus rendering them promising thermoelectric materials. For instance, silicene and germanene possess similar semimetal electronic properties like GE, but their thermal conductivities are orders of magnitude lower. The thermal conductivities of the group VA 2D nanomaterials (phosphorene, arsenene, antimonene and bismuthene) are also much lower than those of other GE-analogous 2D nanomaterials (Table 3). Due to the non-planar lattice structure, the thermal conductivity of group VA 2D nanomaterials is generally low. Moreover, the high anisotropies of their thermal and electrical conductance lead to anisotropic thermoelectric performances with the _ZT_ value along the armchair direction being much larger than that along the zigzag direction [598,599].
